Abstract
We develop an analytical framework for Boolean Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems
(PCSPs) that studies polymorphisms through the notion of influence from Fourier analysis of
Boolean functions. Extending the work of Brakensiek, Guruswami, and Sandeep [ICALP’21]
on Ordered PCSPs, we identify two general phenomena in Boolean minions indicative of hard-
ness or tractability: (1) preservation of coordinate influence under random 2-to-1 minors and
(2) the presence of sharp thresholds. We demonstrate that these phenomena occur in broader
settings than previously established, yielding new hardness/tractability results for minions
consisting of unate or polynomial threshold functions.

Introduction
A key question in theoretical computer science is why some computational problems can be solved
in polynomial time while others remain hard. The computational class NP consists of a vast variety
of computational problems, and currently there is no unified framework that could, for every prob-
lem in NP, explain the underlying mathematical structure that governs its tractability or hardness.
One subclass of NP, for which such a framework does exist is the class of Constraint Satisfaction
Problems (CSPs). In a CSP, the input consists of a set of variables along with constraints on their
values, and the objective is to find an evaluation of the variables satisfying all constraints. The
allowed constraints are usually restricted to a fixed set of relations, known as the CSP template,
defined over a fixed finite domain, called the universe.
CSPs capture many classic computational problems, such as 3-SAT and graph coloring. For
instance, the CSP template for graph coloring consists of a single binary relation: disequality. In
1978, Schaefer showed that, assuming P ̸= NP, every template over a 2-element (Boolean) do-
main defines a CSP which is either NP-hard or solvable in polynomial time [69]. Consequently,
Boolean CSPs contain no NP-intermediate problems. The next milestone was established by Hell
and Neˇsetˇril, who showed that an analogous dichotomy is true for graph CSPs, i.e. whose con-
straints are limited to a single binary and symmetric relation [44]. Several years later, Feder and
2


Vardi conjectured that that the same dichotomy holds for every finite CSP template [33]. Progress
on this conjecture was limited until the development of the algebraic approach to CSPs [46, 45,
24], which analyses CSP complexity via algebraic closure properties of the template, particularly
through multivariate generalizations of endomorphisms known as polymorphisms. This inspired
an active research programme, culminating in 2017 with Bulatov and Zhuk independently proving
the CSP Dichotomy Conjecture [72, 25].
The CSP Dichotomy Theorem tells us that CSPs, which form a rather significant chunk of the
class NP, do not contain NP-intermediate problems. This motivates the question: can the tools
developed for CSPs be used to understand more general subclasses of NP? One extension of CSPs,
which has been gaining a lot of research attention in recent years, is the class of Promise CSPs
(PCSPs) originally introduced in [2], which bridge the gap between decision and approximation
problems by acting as “qualitative” approximation variant of CSPs.
A PCSP template is defined by two sets of constraints: a weak one and a strong one. Given an
instance which is satisfiable with strong constraints, the task is to produce a solution that satisfies
the weak constraints. A well-known example of a PCSP is the Approximate Graph Coloring prob-
lem [41, 51, 29, 42, 15, 9]. In this problem, one is given a graph that is promised to be k-colourable
and must colour it with ℓcolours, where k ≤ℓare fixed parameters. Clearly, the problem is
tractable if k ≤2, but it is conjectured to be NP-hard in all other cases. Despite substantial ef-
fort, this conjecture remains wide open, with only partial cases resolved; the complexity of the
Approximate Graph Coloring is not known1 even for k = 3 and ℓ= 6.
Another important example is PCSP(1in3, NAE) which, given a 3-uniform hypergraph
promised to admit a red/blue coloring in which every hyperedge has exactly one blue vertex, asks
for a red/blue coloring in which no hyperedge is monochromatic. Although separately 1in3-SAT
and NAE-SAT are both NP-hard problems, the aforementioned promise problem is solvable in
polynomial time [16]. Notably, it is also an example of a Boolean PCSP.
A crucial advance in the study of PCSPs was the development of the algebraic approach in
[2, 16, 9]. Similarly to the algebraic theory of CSPs, it focuses on polymorphisms. Given a PCSP
template (A, B), by Pol(A, B) we denote the set of its polymorphisms, which are multivariate ho-
momorphisms from the strong relational structure A to the weak structure B. Most of the existing
results on PCSPs can be understood in terms of the algebraic structure of its template’s polymor-
phisms. In broad terms, a PCSP is usually shown to be tractable if its template admits infinitely
many polymorphisms with no “distinguished” coordinates. Conversely, hardness is usually estab-
lished when every polymorphism possesses a small set of “important” coordinates. For example,
Brakensiek et al. [18] discovered that a PCSP is efficiently solvable if it has infinitely many sym-
metric polymorphisms, that is, which are invariant under permutations of their arguments. On
the other hand, the following multiple choice condition has been widely utilized to obtain hardness
results of multiple PCSPs [2, 16, 35, 54, 19].
Definition (Multiple choice hardness condition [7]). We say that Pol(A, B) satisfies the multiple
choice condition if, there exists C > 0 and a mapping Sel that assigns to each f ∈Pol(A, B) a
subset of its coordinates such that
1. |Sel(f)| ≤C, and

A complete complexity classification of all PCSPs remains open. The history of CSPs suggests
that studying restricted subclasses of PCSP can bring partial results and reveal the underlying
mathematical structure that leads to tractability or hardness. However, even analogues of (1) Hell-
Neˇsetˇril’s dichotomy for graph CSPs and (2) Schaefer’s Boolean CSP dichotomy remain open in
the broader setting of PCSPs.
In this paper, we focus on the latter: Boolean PCSPs. Despite several partial results [2, 20,
16, 35, 17, 5, 3], the complexity classification of all Boolean PCSPs seems to currently be out
of reach. The most general result obtained so far is a complexity dichotomy for the so-called
Ordered Boolean PCSPs (that is, PCSPs that allow to impose inequalities between variables of
the input instance) in [17], conditioned on the recently proposed Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture [21].
The unconditional results are limited and challenging. Therefore, employing perfect-completeness
extensions of Khot’s Unique Games Conjecture [52] — such as Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture [21] or the
d-to-1 Conjecture [52] — as the source of hardness offers a way to bypass the limitations of the
available hardness tools and gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mathematical structure
of hard Boolean PCSPs. In this sense, Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture may serve a role similar to that of
the Unique Games Conjecture in many inapproximability results.
The aforementioned work of [17] on Boolean Ordered PCSPs also pioneered3 the use of Fourier
analysis to study Boolean polymorphisms, although in an indirect way. We believe that using the
full power of Fourier analysis will push the understanding of Boolean PCSPs closer towards re-
solving their complexity classification, and also has the potential to unify most known hardness
and tractability results on Boolean PCSPs. In this paper, the first steps in this direction are pre-
sented. We build the foundation of an analytical framework for studying Boolean PCSPs; as an
application of the new theory, combinatorial arguments of [17] are substituted with our analytical
approach, extending their observations beyond the landscape of Ordered PCSPs.
Coordinate influence
The cornerstone of our research is the notion of influence introduced
in [11], which is one of the most fundamental concepts of Fourier analysis of Boolean functions.
In the simplest setting, for a function f : {0, 1}n →{0, 1}, the influence of a coordinate i ∈[n],
denoted by Infi[f], is the fraction of inputs x ∈{0, 1}n such that flipping the i-th entry xi flips the
output f(x). For example, in the function x 7→maxi xi, each coordinate has influence 21−n, which
is quite small. On the other hand, in the dictatorship function x 7→xi, the dictating coordinate i
has dominating influence 1, while the rest of coordinates are irrelevant — their influence is 0.
As previously mentioned, there seems to be a connection between the PCSP complexity and
occurrence of significant coordinates in its polymorphisms.
Thus, one may surmise that admitting polymorphisms with diminishing maximum influences
characterizes tractability of Boolean PCSPs. Unfortunately, such a guess would be too simplistic
and false. A counterexample is the problem of solving linear equations over Z2, which is solvable
in poly-time by standard Gaussian Elimination. However, the only non-trivial polymorphisms

Subclasses of Boolean PCSPs
As the understanding of all Boolean PCSPs is still shallow, the
research community has been focusing on smaller classes, enforcing structural or algebraic re-
strictions on PCSP templates.
For Boolean PCSPs, the first substantial work in this direction was the conditional dichotomy
for Ordered PCSPs of [17]. In algebraic terms, these PCSPs amount to restricting the polymor-
phisms to increasing functions4, i.e., such that f(x) ≤f(y) for any pair of tuples x ≤y5. This
was followed by the work in [5], where the authors provided a complete complexity dichotomy
for Linear Threshold PCSPs. These are PCSPs whose all polymorphisms are linear threshold func-
tions, which take the form P ai · xi > t. In this paper, we investigate through an analytic lens the
following two extensions of Ordered and Linear Threshold PCSPs:
1. Unate PCSPs are Boolean PCSPs whose polymorphisms are all unate functions, meaning that
each coordinate is increasing or decreasing: a coordinate i of a function f : {0, 1}n →{0, 1}
is increasing if f(a1, . . . , 0, . . . , an) ≤f(a1, . . . , 1, . . . , an) for every a1, . . . , an ∈{0, 1}; it
is decreasing if the inequality is reversed. Unate functions have been prominent in switching
theory [59], computational learning theory [34], and complexity theory [4]. Austrin, H˚astad
and Martinsson [3] have recently investigated unate functions in the context of PCSPs from a
combinatorial perspective.
2. Polynomial Threshold PCSPs are PCSPs whose polymorphisms are bounded-degree polyno-
mial threshold functions (PTFs), meaning that each such polymorphism can be represented as
the sign of a bounded-degree real multilinear polynomial Q. While PTFs have been extensively
studied in learning theory [71, 1, 10, 53, 64] and from structural and extremal perspectives [40,
63, 43, 28, 50, 49], Polynomial Threshold PCSPs remain unexplored in their full generality.

2. Sharp thresholds imply tractability. Sharp threshold is a phenomenon where a property
of a random system transitions from being almost certainly absent to almost certainly present
over a negligible change in a parameter.
In the context of Boolean functions, we are interested in the property “f(x) = 1“.
The tractability result of [17] essentially asserts that an Ordered PCSP is solvable in poly-time
as long as its polymorphisms admit a sharp threshold. We demonstrate that a similar connec-
tion arises in the larger class of Unate PCSPs, with an appropriately defined notion of sharp
threshold.
Theorem 1.2 (Informal). Suppose that (A, B) is a Unate PCSP template. If Pol(A, B) admits a
sharp threshold, then PCSP(A, B) is solvable in polynomial time.
The study of sharp threshold behavior occupies a central role in probabilistic combinatorics and
statistical physics. The formal mathematical investigation began in the late 1950s, when Erd¨os
and R´enyi discovered that many properties of random graphs (e.g. connectivity or appearance
of a “giant component”) do not emerge gradually as the density increases but rather depend on
it in a “sharp threshold manner” [31, 32]. In fact, the later works of Bollob´as and Thomason
[13], as well as Friedgut and Kalai [39], proved that every monotone graph property exhibits a
sharp threshold behavior7.
Sharp threshold behavior can also be observed in computational complexity theory, for the tran-
sition from “easy” to “hard” computational problems is usually abrupt. For example, Friedgut
[38] discovered that the satisfiability probability of a random k-CNF formula on n variables
exhibits a sharp threshold when the “clause density” increases. In particular, sufficiently sparse
k-CNF formulas are almost always satisfiable, while sufficiently dense ones are almost never
satisfiable. Therefore the hardest formulas are those with “clause density” close to this critical
threshold point.

Related work
There have been attempts at obtaining an analytical proof of the CSP Dichotomy
since 2009 (see [55, 23]). So far, these attempts have had limited success.
To our knowledge, Libor Barto was the first to suggest studying PCSP polymorphisms using
analytical tools. In particular, he showed how to obtain a symmetric threshold function of any
arity from any cyclic increasing function of sufficiently large arity as an identification minor [6].
This was later incorporated into the proof of a conditional dichotomy for Boolean Ordered PCSPs
by Brakensiek et al. [17].
Another notable contribution on Boolean PCSPs, although not relying on Fourier analysis, is
the dichotomy for Linear Threshold PCSPs established by Banakh and Kozik [5].
Beyond the Boolean domain, Braverman et al. [22] recently provided a general pipeline which,
given a perfect-completeness dictatorship test for a CSP template, produces a reduction from the
Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture to the problem of approximating (quantitatively) the corresponding CSP.
Although not directly focused on PCSPs, their hardness analysis shares several features with our
results in Section 3.

Unate PCSPs
In the previous section, we illustrated how a sharp threshold in a minion of increasing functions
leads to tractability. Sharp threshold is an abstract concept, so it is natural to expect that “sharp
threshold implies tractability” holds in more general minions that exhibit some relaxed notion of
monotonicity.
In this section, we study unate functions. We denote the set of increasing coordinates of a unate
function by dom↑(f ), and the set of decreasing coordinates by dom↓(f ). A function f is unate if

dom↑(f) ∪dom↓(f) = [ar(f)]. Note that dom↑(f) ∩dom↓(f) are exactly those coordinates on
which f does not depend.
A simple example of a unate function is (x, y) 7→x(1 −y). A more practical example is an

Conclusions
We initiated an analytical framework for studying Boolean polymorphisms, building on tools from
the Fourier analysis of Boolean functions. Substantially generalizing [17, Lemma 4.4], we proved
the Influence Preservation Lemma, which yields a family of PCSP hardness reductions from the
Rich 2-to-1 Gap Label Cover problem, conjectured to be NP-hard [21, 17], to Unate and Polynomial
Threshold PCSPs whose polymorphisms do not admit diminishing maximal coordinate influences.
Furthermore, we introduced the notion of a sharp threshold for unate functions and investigated
its relation to tractable Unate PCSPs, directly extending [17, Lemma 3.4].
We view our main contribution as the establishment of a general analytic framework for
Boolean PCSPs, which will hopefully be further developed to amplify the algebraic approach [9]
and advance the understanding of the largely unexplored Boolean PCSP landscape.
Several questions that arose during the investigation of particular subclasses of Boolean PCSPs
remain open. For Unate PCSPs, we gave sufficient conditions for tractability in Theorem 5.12 and
hardness in Theorem 5.15.
Question 1. Do Theorem 5.12 and Theorem 5.15 fully characterize the complexity of all Unate PCSPs?

In this section, we outline the reduction from the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture, recently postulated by
[21], to any PCSP satisfying our random 2-to-1 condition. This reduction is encapsulated in The-

The reduction follows a standard framework established in [2, 16, 9]; in particular, it splits into
two parts, reducing to an intermediate problem first.
E.1
Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture
The Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture followed from the long-standing quest for a perfect-completeness ana-
log of the Unique Games Conjecture, which asserts that it is NP-hard to determine the approximate
value of a certain type of game, known as a Unique Game. In the literature, these games are usually
formalized by means of Label Cover.
Definition (Label Cover). An instance of Label Cover Ψ = (L ∪R, E, ΣL, ΣR, Π) consists of a
bipartite graph (L ∪R, E), alphabets [ΣL], [ΣR] and a set Π of functional constraints πe : [ΣL] →
73


[ΣR] for every e ∈E. Given a labeling σ, which assigns an element of [ΣL] to every vertex in L
and an element of [ΣR] to every vertex in R, we say that constraint πe ∈Π for e = (u, v) ∈E is
satisfied if πe(σ(u)) = σ(v). The value of Ψ is the maximum fraction of constraints that a labeling
can satisfy simultaneously.
Unique games correspond to Label Cover instances where all πe are bijective functions; simi-
larly, 2-to-1 games correspond to Label Cover instances where all πe are 2-to-1 maps. The Unique
Games Conjecture postulates that it is NP-hard to find the value of Ψ, even under the promise that
this value is smaller than a fixed δ < 1. We usually formalize these promise problems under the
name of Gap Label Cover.
Definition (Gap Label Cover). Suppose that n ≥1 and 0 ≤ε ≤δ ≤1. By Gap-Label-Covern[δ, ε]
we denote the decision problem defined as follows: Given a Label Cover instance Ψ with ΣL, ΣR ≤
n, answer YES if there is a labeling satisfying at least a δ-fraction of constraints, and answer NO
if all labelings satisfy at most an ε-fraction of constraints.
For PCSP applications, one usually requires that δ = 1, which makes it a perfect-completeness
problem. Finally, we define Rich Games.
Definition (Richness). An instance Ψ of Label Cover is Rich 2-to-1 if
• all constraints πe are 2-to-1 maps, and
• the process of uniformly choosing a constraint adjacent to any fixed vertex in L yields the uni-
form distribution over all 2-to-1 maps [2n] →[n].29

Abstract: We develop an analytical framework for Boolean Promise Constraint Satisfaction Problems (PCSPs) that studies polymorphisms through the notion of influence from Fourier analysis of Boolean functions. Extending the work of Brakensiek, Guruswami, and Sandeep [ICALP’21] on Ordered PCSPs, we identify two general phenomena in Boolean minions indicative of hard- ness or tractability: (1) preservation of coordinate influence under random 2-to-1 minors and (2) the presence of sharp thresholds. We demonstrate that these phenomena occur in broader settings than previously established, yielding new hardness/tractability results for minions consisting of unate or polynomial threshold functions.
